thread.title: Jim Sloan Positions For 2019: Keeping JPMorgan, Extending Maturities With 2 Fixed-Income Anomalies, Resolving To Keep Cool - JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM)

author: Jim Sloan
title: Jim Sloan Positions For 2019: Keeping JPMorgan, Extending Maturities With 2 Fixed-Income Anomalies, Resolving To Keep Cool - JPMorgan Chase & Co. (NYSE:JPM)
text:
Q. What do you expect to be the key driver of stock market performance in 2019? If you focus on a specific asset class, please address what will be the key driver? Every positive thing envisioned by optimistic forecasters a year ago actually came to pass in 2018, but two strong market rallies were followed by 10% corrections, which gave the rallies back and left the market as I write slightly down for the year. One could argue that the reason for this is the list of currently popular suspects - trade war with China, flattening yield curve, and political/economic issues in Europe - but a very important reason flew under the radar: a partial normalization of price-earnings ratios. A key question for 2019 is whether this downward trend in valuations will continue. Many argue that the current PE of the S&P 500 (about 20) has improved and makes the market statistically cheap, especially with strong earnings increases expected again next year. It's important to keep in mind that market PE broke out above its historical average during the 1990s and has not returned to its historical normal average of about 15. Both market highs and market lows have occurred at higher valuations than in the past.
Are we living in a permanent new era? The answer to that question is almost always the same: probably not. You could make the case that the low-interest-rate environment of the past 10 years changed things. Even Buffett buys into the idea that low rates justify paying up a bit for stocks. Relatively low rates may stick around for a while, but rates do have directional moves over long cycles. A new long cycle of rising rates may have begun in late 2015, but if it resembles the last such rate cycle, 1941 to 1982, rates may move up slowly for quite a while. Sooner or later, however, the new environment will likely cause market PE to shift downward.
The present trailing PE of about 20 for the S&P 500 is consistent with market peaks in that earlier low rate period, not with market bottoms or great buying opportunities. Thanks to great demographics, growth in that era was much more vigorous than in the present while inflation was similarly low until the late 1960s. Summing up these factors, it's hard to see how the market going forward 10 years or so can achieve the historical return of 10% most investors have in their heads. As I suggested at this time last year, future returns going out that far are likely to be more like 4-6%, if not lower. I wrote a more detailed historical piece on this subject on May 22 examining some historical data, which suggests the market might be approaching a "Little Ice Age." A normalization of average PE will probably move at the barely observable speed of a receding glacier, but the effects on shorter-term market weather can be severe.
While I have a fair degree of confidence in this estimate of the long-term future, it doesn't have much predictive power for one year. It just cautions that the market may have begun to feel the undertow of a long-term tide going out on equity valuations. The short answer to the question about market performance in 2019 is that it depends upon how much money companies earn and what sort of multiple investors will be willing to pay for those earnings. The economy is strong, but there is some evidence that the cost of inputs may soon begin to impact all-time high corporate profit margins. The behavior of interest rates will be the major factor in what investors are willing to pay for earnings.
Q. As we approach 2019, are you bullish or bearish on U.S. stocks? Like last year, I am neither bull nor bear. Hoping to live another 30 years (current age 74), I am always bullish on the long term. For the short term, I have never held a strong opinion except at market extremes. When the market was outrageously expensive as it was around 2000, I was a short-term bear and very wrong for a year or two. This view was eventually very right in a way that more than made up for looking silly for a year or two. When the market was dirt cheap in the 1970s, I was persistently bullish and nobody wanted to hear it.
The structure of my portfolio speaks to my current ambivalence. I am currently 50% in equities; all individual stocks. I first got down to 50% stocks in 2016 - too early, of course, but with a little luck came very close to equaling the S&P 500 in both 2016 and 2017. This year the market is down slightly, and so am I. If the market struck me as extraordinarily cheap, I might go to as much as 90% in stocks.
Q. Seeking Alpha readers always like specific suggestions, and a primary ticker is always welcome in SA articles. Do you have one? The answer is yes, but first a disclaimer. I used to be amused but mildly irritated in the old days when Barron's used to conduct and feature short-term stock-picking contests. The reason these contests bothered me was that I seriously doubt that any significant number of investors have gotten rich and stayed rich or even insured a comfortable retirement by nailing a single pick. That's especially true of short-term trading picks. The only way a single stock pick has worked wonders for accumulation of wealth has been the occasion when an investor had the good luck or special insight to buy into one of the great long-term growth stories at an early stage. A year is too short a period for that kind of growth to have its magical effect. For myself, I'm sure I'll never profit from a short-term trade in a way that moves the needle.
I'll tell you an amusing story. A couple of my very smart tennis students were taking a high school investment course which included a stock picking contest and asked for my advice. The contest was to last something like a month. I told them that I didn't have a clue about a rational answer to their question, but if they could make a pair, I could suggest a strategy making it highly probable that one of the two of them would win the contest. The other would almost certainly come in last. I suggested that one of them buy a triple leveraged bullish ETF, it may have been the QQQs, and the other buy the triple leveraged bearish version. The idea amused them, and they did it, with the expected results. Their teacher wasn't amused. He threatened to give them bad grades on the contest. I told them at first just to explain that they happened to have opposite opinions. When that didn't fly, I suggested that they explain to the teacher why the contest was silly and at cross purposes with the presumed objective of the course - a serious introduction to the kind of investing which would work over a lifetime. They got their well-earned As.
Forgive me, then, if my single stock idea is a bit dull. It's JPMorgan ( JPM ). JPM barely noses out Bank of America ( BAC ). Both are dirt cheap. Both have outstanding CEOs with long experience and outstanding understanding of their industry and the economy as a whole. Both have good dividends and the opportunity to return far more capital via buybacks than most companies. Having low price-to-book value ratios, their buybacks will currently take place at highly accretive prices. Both banks are compounding machines. JPMorgan is the slightly more conservative pick and also slightly more expensive, though still dirt cheap. BAC has somewhat greater exposure to a reduction in net interest margin (NIM) due to a flattening yield curve.
Both BAC and JPM are dull choices. Dull is good. To be honest, though, I have no idea how JPM or BAC will do over exactly one year, although I believe both will serve a serious investor splendidly over five years.
The beauty of JPMorgan is really how well it fits into a long-term portfolio as a stock likely to perform better than the market for many years with relatively low risk. Because of the last market disaster, the market is still a little nuts about the riskiness of banks. Financials are the cheapest area of the market not issuing a death rattle. My portfolio is strongly tilted toward banks and industrials and I own both JPM and BAC in significant size, along with a legacy position in Wells Fargo ( WFC ). I recently sold Citigroup ( C ) in a Rollover IRA in order to make room for attractive brokered bank CDs and replaced it in a regular taxable account with BAC (for IRS purposes, in order to start with a fresh cost basis). I will add that I took into account the fact that Citi has the most international exposure of the major banks. I did not sell JPMorgan, which I held in the same IRA.
I gave serious consideration to making Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A )( BRK.B ) my single stock recommendation. It is by far my largest holding at about 20% of the equity side in family accounts. It seems fairly valued to slightly cheap at its current price around $200 on the B shares. Berkshire is essentially a best-of-breed conglomerate/mutual fund with an unequaled record in capital allocation and outstanding shareholder friendliness. Buffett seems healthy and vital, and Berkshire seems the same and has been constructed to prosper long after his departure. It is not as diversified as the S&P 500, but one of its virtues is actually what it omits. If I have a mad moment in a major market decline, I can always go out and get more fully diversified by buying what seem to be the best of the tech stocks and the FANGs. Don't hold your breath for that, though.
In the end, JPMorgan was just cheaper than Berkshire. One indication of that might be seen in the action of Buffett himself. His 13F from the third quarter showed that he bought four billion bucks worth of JPM (and added about the same amount to his BAC position, for that matter). This amounted to a statement by Buffett that shares of the two banks seemed to him cheaper than those of his own company.
A passing issue with Berkshire is that unless things change between now and the end of the year, its earnings for the fourth quarter are likely to be pulled down sharply by market declines in its publicly traded portfolio. The recent decline in Apple ( AAPL ) and several financials will likely reduce the overall value of his portfolio by as much as $14 billion, and under rules originating from the new tax law, that reduction will be reflected on Berkshire's fourth quarter and annual income statements. The portfolio losses will be partially offset by perhaps $6 billion in operating income, but reported income for the fourth quarter may still be a net loss of about $8 billion. This doesn't bother me at all when it comes to the long-term health of Berkshire. It would, however, produce a decline in book value sufficiently large to virtually wipe out the increases of the first three quarters of the year. Because book value is an important factor in the price Buffett sets for buybacks of Berkshire shares, his hurdle for buybacks may go up a bit. That buyback hurdle, of course, serves as an implicit floor for the stock price and has been the source of positive asymmetry between Berkshire's potential upside and potential downside.
I have very few worries about how JPMorgan and other banks will perform despite some shrinking of NIM due to the flat yield curve. Earnings are very unlikely to decline radically even with a fully (3 months to 30 years) inverted yield curve and recession. Inverted yield curves reverse themselves fairly quickly. My bigger concerns about the future of major banks have involved risks to the basic business model coming from fintech, blockchain, and the preference of millennials for alternative payment intermediaries. Over the past year, however, I have become more confident that the large banks, and especially JPM and BAC, are well aware of these challenges and have used their tremendous resources to get themselves positioned out in front of them. For value, stability, and dependable moderate growth for the long term, and a high probability of outperforming the market over any period longer than a couple of years, I suggest JPMorgan as a stalwart for any portfolio of individual stocks.
Q. How does the political climate affect the risks and opportunities for next year? Most aspects of any political climate end up having very little effect on the markets. Even the name-calling and nastiness of gridlock seem to many observers a neutral to positive thing. Only a few political events could have a serious impact on the market or the economy. One that should be obvious, but is not often mentioned, would be any loss of the independence of the Federal Reserve. The Fed is a bit like the judiciary. Whatever you think of Fed policy in a particular instance, the existence of an independent and technically grounded monetary authority is fundamental to a modern economy.
Trade wars are awful, of course, but one reason we are in the middle of one is a gradual increase in grievances which occurred while the world changed and the U.S. did little to defend its own interests in the new global economy. It's obviously not a good idea to pull down the pillars like Samson and collapse the whole temple, but a little pushback isn't necessarily a bad idea. Trade disagreements in North America appear to have been straightened out already, but trade disagreements with the EU and China are more difficult. The toughest issues are the disadvantageous terms under which American companies must operate in China and the required surrender of proprietary technologies in ways that at times may threaten U.S. national security. We have to fix that. Nevertheless, I expect the trade issues to be resolved over the course of 2019. Neither we nor the Chinese have any interest in blowing up the economic world. A trade war is something like a labor-management dispute. Once a strike is declared, the next headline is going to be a settlement.
The one political possibility, with probability perhaps as high as 25%, is a protracted and ugly presidential impeachment process. With a do-over due in 2020 no rational person of whatever political viewpoint should want that. I have witnessed two such processes in my adult life, the Clinton impeachment, which didn't amount to much, and the Nixon impeachment and resignation, which coincided with very dark times in the U.S. The Nixon process took place as the U.S. sank into terrible stagflation and an inflationary bear market (1973-74). One can argue whether the basic arrow of causation ran from the economy to Nixon's impeachment process or vice versa. Having written my undergraduate history honors thesis on Nixon (in 1968), I had followed his career closely and thought his impeachment might not have taken place without a painful economic downturn as the background. Who knows? It was probably a feedback loop contributing to a terrible downward spiral.
I don't know how many Americans would actually rally to Trump, but I think quite a few might as the hard hats did for Nixon. Unlike Nixon, I doubt that the current President would go gently into that good night. There would be a very real risk of a Constitutional crisis. Nothing good would come from any of this whatever the outcome.
Q. Do you expect the yield curve to continue flattening in 2019, and if so, what impact will that have on the equity market and the economy in general? There really isn't much space left for flattening. It's flat already in intermediate maturities. It may continue to flatten further out on the curve. It may even invert significantly, with the sort of inversion which clearly implies a coming recession. On the other hand, the economy might conceivably pick up after a pause. With deficits about to set a series of all-time records, the Treasury will need to sell an increasing number of bonds and that in itself may cause the yield curve to hold its current shape on the long end. On balance, I think that economic growth is slowing, inflation is slight, and the largest probability lies with a flatter and ultimately inverted yield curve. Foreign demand for longer U.S. bonds will likely continue from countries with much lower yields. If the yield curve did steepen sharply, that might be the big surprise of the year. I'm not betting on it. In a modest way, I'm betting against it.
Q. In terms of asset allocation, how are you positioned heading into the New Year? As I mentioned above, I am standing pat with a 50/50 equity/fixed portfolio. That continues a neutral view of the world going back three years. Over that period, I was happy to get half the market return on the equity side in exchange for lower risk. The major change I have made looking ahead to 2019 involves a decision that it's time to get more return out of the fixed income side by extending maturities.
At the beginning of 2018, the entirety of my fixed income portfolio consisted of Vanguard money market funds, both taxable and tax exempt. Their yields had been steadily rising along with Fed rate hikes with about a one-month lag time. In May, I decided that it was time to lock in rates to a limited extent. I used brokered bank CDs with 18- and 24-month maturities, both yielding more than T-Notes at the equivalent maturity. I set this November/December as the time to reevaluate this process. I could have just extended the 2-year ladder, but instead I made an important decision to extend maturities quickly over the entire range of maturities. This led to my most important and most unexpected action of 2018. It all happened over two or three weeks.
In November, the world changed. It seems possible that the rate cycle might have begun to turn. The Fed may have listened to the President or it may have noticed that the cycle of rate hikes had begun to cause some softness in longer-term economic indicators, suggesting more of a wait-and-see approach. The Fed narrative has subtly changed. The rise in rates stalled out across the curve and started to drop. I wasn't sure if this trend reversal would persist, and I still am not, but it was enough to prompt a decisive action.
From my perspective, this really changed nothing on the equity side. I didn't like the PE of the S&P index, but I liked the inexpensive value stocks in my own portfolio just fine. On the fixed side, however, everything had changed. I decided to lock in yields over the short to intermediate term and find a way to extend maturities to the long end. What I wanted to end up with was something close to a conventional fixed income allocation with a full range of maturities and enough cash for flexibility. Two anomalies helped me achieve this.
The first anomaly was in brokered bank CDs, bank CDs sold at a discount to brokerages for resale. They had popped up on my Vanguard brokerage accounts, and I had paid close attention to their characteristics when I bought a couple in May. They can be purchased on the same terms as all CDs with a $250K FDIC guarantee per owner per bank. By the time I was ready to take a major action, an anomaly stared me in the face. After the offering period, these CDs trade in the open market - a convenience if you should desperately need to exit the position - but during the offering period the rates are fixed. What that meant was that outstanding rates - 3.25% on the 3-year and 3.55% on the five year - continued to be offered as the yield on corresponding Treasuries sank like a stone, as much as 30 basis points. As a result, those two CDs paid about 50 and 80 basis points, respectively, more than the corresponding Treasuries. I'll take that any day on vehicles which have the maturities I want and are essentially as safe as Treasuries.
The second anomaly existed in the long-term muni market. Munis ought to trade with a yield lower than Treasuries, and they currently do on the short end. The anomaly is on the longer end. There are reasons for it, mainly that munis trade on their own reasons, such as changing estimates of the value of the tax-exemption versus the small increase in risk, including the risk of different tax policies in the distant future. These reasons don't seem to justify the fact that at approximately 15 years out, the yield curve of AA-rated munis crosses the yield curve of Treasuries, reaching parity. The tax advantage is effectively free. At longer durations than 15 years, the yields of AA munis are higher than those of Treasuries, the difference increasing to as much as 60 basis points around 30 years.
You can keep up with events in the muni-bond market by reading authoritative SA pieces by David Kotok of Cumberland Advisors, a heavyweight in institutional money management. I don't feel able to buy individual munis - to my mind that's a game for professional specialists. Instead I went through Vanguard funds looking for a fund which had the characteristics I wanted. The closest was the Long-Term Tax Exempt Fund Admiral Shares ( VWLUX ). It is centered in AA munis (45.7%), with 16.7% in AAA and 24.2% in A. The percentage of holdings in 10-20 year munis is about 44.5% while 20-30 year munis are at 33.6% and 4% is in bonds with maturities of 30 years plus. My estimate is that at least half the portfolio consists of bonds with yields above parity with Treasuries.
Sorry for being a little wonky, but what this anomaly adds up to is a reasonable probability of a win-win outcome. There is a good likelihood of getting a coupon yield well above 3%, with a tax equivalent yield, you can calculate by deducting from the coupon yield your marginal state tax rate and then dividing by 1 minus your marginal Federal tax rate. There's a fairly good chance the muni yield advantage over Treasuries will close as it has in the past. The upshot: even if long rates rise and long Treasuries go down in price, long munis should go down much less and possibly even rally.
What I ended up with was a barbell of munis - short-term money market plus long-term bonds, along with a ladder of CDs with yields exceeding maturities of equivalent Treasuries. That's a pretty conventional fixed income portfolio, but with kickers provided by the slightly unconventional mix of vehicles. It was a big step for me personally, as I haven't owned a long bond since owning a few 25-year Treasury Zeroes back in the 1980s.
You probably won't find the same batch of brokered bank CDs available at this point, but you might form the habit of checking Vanguard from time to time to see if there might be a similar anomaly. The long-term muni fund is there for your own inspection, and you should do the calculations of taxable-equivalent yield for your own tax bracket.
Q. What "surprise" do you see in the market that currently isn't getting sufficient investor attention? Hiding in plain sight is the fact that several major countries are already in or on the brink of recession and have bear markets well underway in their equity markets. China is probably in what, for China, is a recession. Likewise Japan. Germany just had a negative quarter of economic growth. In almost every country in the EU, the 10-year sovereign bond is trading at a negative rate between 1% and 2%. That means investors are so afraid of the future they are willing to pay their governments to hold their money. The UK is in a terrible lose-lose situation. How long can this go on without affecting us? So far Americans have been able to dismiss the rest of the world and say, in effect, "I'm okay, you're screwed up." This could be the year in which the rest of the world drags the U.S. down. It's like what happens to a good stock in a bear market. The old market aphorism goes: "When they raid the cathouse they take all the girls and the piano player too." The U.S. is like that one good stock - maybe the piano player. Could this be the year they put the U.S. into the back of the paddy wagon with the others?
Q. What role will the Fed play in the coming year? There are folks who would pay a million bucks to know the answer to that one, but I can't help them. Best guess: yes to a rate hike in December, then possibly a pause, or possibly another hike, and then a pause. After the pause, the odds are that a year or a bit more passes while the Fed continues to assess the situation. Further rate increases will happen only if the economy and inflation heat up.
Q. What issue is receiving too much attention or is already priced in? Probably the trade war and the eccentricities of the President unless both ramp up to a higher level. I suggest to my wife several times a day to stop focusing on her displeasure with Trump and focus on her business, actual economic conditions, and the pleasures of everyday life.
Q. What current trends or fads strike you as badly thought through? For the life of me, I can't get my head around Bitcoin or the FIRE movement. Is 74 just too old to understand the world? Bitcoin can't possibly serve as a currency or a commodity, so what is it? Soldiers when I was in the military used to say, "If you can't eat it, have intimate relations with it, or rest under the shade of it, what good is it?" (Soldier language was saltier in those days, but I'm sure the New Army has cleaned up soldier talk). Bitcoin, in any case, fails on all of the above criteria. All I can think of by way of description for it is an electronic tulip bulb. My commiseration to the young and innocent who went for it. Anything with a chart like that is probably headed toward zero. What can the bottom possibly be other than zero? It's dead, and the chart will approach the x axis as a limit. Oh, never mind me on that subject. I'm a card-carrying old fogy.
As for the FIRE movement, I totally get the part about Financial Independence. Financial Independence is about being able to deal with the unexpected, look after those you care about, and have the privilege of only doing work you like and telling people where to go if you feel like it. But the other half of FIRE seems to represent an underlying cultural change. The implications disturb me. Sudden idleness around the age of forty never had any attraction for me. My wife tells me that she once thought she wanted to retire at 40, but she sounds like she's describing an idle daydream of a naive and younger self rather than a serious program. She owns a small business and is working harder than ever at age 63, although she doesn't have to. She loves every minute of it, including the pleasure of complaining about parts of it.
Retirement as a concept has an interestingly brief history. It didn't really exist until about two hundred years ago. Roman soldiers who survived to middle age got pensions, and so did the English veterans of Waterloo, but those are exceptions I can understand. Most people in a mainly agrarian world worked until they couldn't, then suffered through a couple of years of frailty and died. To a large extent, they were taken care of by family and neighbors, although a few tribal societies like the Inuit left the elderly on the side of the trail with a knife to fight off the wolves and bears. I think I could have accepted either of those outcomes if I had grown up in one of those cultures.
From a purely practical standpoint, FIRE aspirants should draw up a time line of the past 50 or 60 years, sit down for an hour, and think about it. Whew! Lots of events, including more than a decade of serious inflation. Is your portfolio ready to handle that? I'm not sure mine is, even with much shorter expected lifespan and carefully diversified assets. Are you really, really prepared to take the chance?
What I truly can't understand is why a healthy person would want to stop being a productive human being when life is probably less than half over. There's something reductive and pessimistic in wishing to remove oneself from the day-to-day interactions with people and the problem solving that comes with work. I can't imagine a life that doesn't involve dealing with challenges, tough choices, and adversity.
FIRE seems to be a generational thing among the young. I worry about the implications. Does it represent a deep unwillingness to be fully engaged with the real world? Is it a negative statement on the everyday activities of ordinary people? How many people with disabilities would leap at the chance to engage with the world more fully in productive work? How many permanently unemployed unskilled workers would leap to enjoy the rewards working provides in self-esteem and self-definition as well as money?
The idea of working more years rather than fewer, if one is able to, could be part of the solution to the problems with Social Security, which mainly stem from neglecting to factor in increasing lifespans and pegging the full retirement point way too early. That's not my main reason for continuing to work, however. I feel lucky every morning when I am able to jump out of bed and teach a few hours of tennis first to adults and later to kids. They make up my tribal community, as Seeking Alpha also does in a slightly different way. I appreciate the several work environments where I can interact with a variety of people who share my interests. These jobs help me continue to have a productive life and feel that I am adding something of value to the world. I worry about the future of a society in which people specifically want to avoid making a contribution. I don't look forward to the day when I won't be able to do these things any more.
Q. Is there a single predominant theme to bear in mind when handling your financial life in 2019? Napoleon once said - I can't for the life of me find the quote, so help me if you have it - that the value of a common soldier came not from doing heroic and exceptional things but from doing "the normal thing" while everyone around him was going crazy. This accords with a few memories I have from Vietnam.
Sticking to "the normal thing" even amidst tumult and crazy behavior is a pretty good foundation for actions in the financial markets. I think it will be especially important in 2019. Stick to basically correct allocations and methods and ignore the hurly-burly that surrounds you. Don't try to be a hero. Take what the market gives you. Don't reach for yields. Make necessary changes that are well-thought-out. Avoid major impulsive actions. Just do the normal thing.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BRK.B, JPM, BAC, WFC, VWLUX.
